title: Use of BGP for Routing in Large-Scale Data Centers
summary: This informational document describes how some operators use BGP as the sole routing protocol in very large data centers, where simplicity of operation matters a great deal. It covers design choices such as the network topology, address assignment and routing configuration used in this approach. It is a description of practice rather than a new protocol.

eli5.summary: In a huge building with many hallways, signs keep people from getting lost. This describes how a big data center can use one familiar routing system for all its signs, which keeps things simple.

questions: using ebgp as the only data center routing protocol
subtitle: Routing large server farms with BGP instead of traditional switching

tldr.problem: Warehouse-scale data centers with hundreds of thousands of servers need network designs that can scale horizontally by adding identical switches, not by upgrading them, while keeping operations simple.
tldr.mechanism: Use a flat Clos (folded fat-tree) topology where all switches are the same type, and run External BGP (EBGP) as the only routing protocol, avoiding the complexity of multiple protocols or centralized control.
tldr.outcome: This approach has been proven in large deployments and enables scaling to very large sizes while keeping the network easy to operate and maintain with a small team.

today: RFC 7938 is an Informational RFC that remains current and widely referenced in the data center industry. It has not been obsoleted and continues to document a proven approach to large-scale data center networking that is used by major Internet operators.

sections.title: Scaling Data Center Networks
sections.content:
Large data centers operate at warehouse scale, supporting more than one hundred thousand servers in a single facility. These environments need networks that can handle enormous amounts of server-to-server traffic (called "east-west" traffic) in addition to traffic going in and out of the data center ("north-south" traffic).

Traditional tree-based network designs cannot scale to this size without becoming expensive or hitting physical limits. The RFC describes how operators at large scale build and run data centers using BGP as the sole routing protocol. This design prioritizes operational simplicity and network stability so that a small team can manage the entire network effectively.

This is not a new protocol design but rather a description of proven operational practice.
sections.eli5: A huge company warehouse needs to move packages efficiently between all the workers. The usual switching design breaks down. This describes a better way that has actually worked.

sections.title: Design Requirements for Large Scale
sections.content:
The RFC identifies five key requirements. First, the topology must scale horizontally by adding more identical links and switches, not by upgrading the switches themselves. This keeps capital costs down and allows infinite scaling.

Second, only a narrow set of standard features should be required from different vendors' equipment. This maximizes choice and competition while ensuring interoperability.

Third, the routing protocol must be simple to implement and operate, not complex or hard to understand.

Fourth, failure domains must be minimized so that when something breaks, it affects as few devices as possible. Ethernet networks with large Layer 2 domains are susceptible to broadcast storms that can bring down entire networks, so routing (Layer 3) is preferred.

Fifth, the design must support some traffic engineering, ideally by giving operators explicit control over which path carries which traffic. This helps with load balancing and distributing traffic across available paths.
sections.eli5: Add more hallways without rebuilding them. Use standard equipment from different makers. Keep routing simple. Don't have big broadcast storms. Let operators control traffic flow.

sections.title: Topology: Traditional Tree versus Clos
sections.content:
Traditional data center topologies use a tree structure with three layers: Tier 1 (core), Tier 2 (aggregation), and Tier 3 (access). As you move up the tree, switches have higher port density and capacity. This works for mostly external traffic, but it cannot scale for massive server-to-server traffic without expensive upgrades.

The RFC recommends a folded Clos topology (also called "leaf-spine" or "fat-tree"), which uses uniform switches at two main levels: Tier 1 (spine) switches in the middle, and Tier 2 (leaf) switches at the edges connected to servers. All switches are identical, allowing horizontal scaling. The topology is fully non-blocking or slightly oversubscribed, meaning traffic between servers can use any available path without contention.

Tier 1 switches have exactly one path to every server, which is an important property for routing. The topology can be scaled further by adding more stages in a 5-stage or higher Clos design.
sections.eli5: Instead of one big tree with a thick trunk, use a web of identical switches. Every hallway has the same capacity. Add more switches without changing anything else.

sections.title: Using EBGP as the Routing Protocol
sections.content:
The RFC argues for EBGP (External BGP) as the sole routing protocol in the data center. Each switch is assigned an Autonomous System Number (ASN), even though all switches are in the same organization. Tier 2 (leaf) switches advertise host or prefix routes upward, and Tier 1 (spine) switches advertise routes downward.

Benefits of this approach include simplicity (only one protocol to operate), vendor interoperability (BGP is standard and widely supported), and operational familiarity (network operators already know BGP from the Internet backbone). The RFC recommends using private ASNs from the reserved ranges.

Each Tier 2 switch peers with multiple Tier 1 switches, creating multiple paths. BGP's path selection and ECMP (Equal Cost Multipath) spread traffic across all available paths, providing load balancing and resilience.
sections.eli5: Use the same routing system that the Internet uses, but inside the data center. Every switch can talk to every other switch about which ways work best.

sections.title: Equal Cost Multipath and Traffic Distribution
sections.content:
In a Clos topology, multiple equal-cost paths typically exist between any two endpoints. ECMP allows switches to load-balance traffic across these paths. When a switch has multiple BGP routes with the same cost, it can forward traffic across all of them, distributing the load.

The RFC discusses basic ECMP, ECMP across multiple ASNs (different upstream choices), and weighted ECMP where some paths carry more traffic than others. For applications that need very fine-grained control, consistent hashing can be used to ensure the same flow always takes the same path, avoiding out-of-order delivery.
sections.eli5: Traffic can take many routes at once. The switches split traffic fairly among them so no single path gets overloaded.

sections.title: Routing Convergence and Failure Recovery
sections.content:
When a link or switch fails, the network must converge (update routes) quickly. In a Clos topology, failures are detected relatively quickly through BGP keepalives and timers. Tier 1 switches detect a downed link within seconds, and other switches learn of the failure through BGP updates.

The RFC notes that the Clos topology itself limits failure impact. A single downed Tier 2 switch affects only the servers connected to that switch. A downed Tier 1 spine switch does not cause complete loss of connectivity (multiple spines exist) but may create a traffic bottleneck if other paths become congested.

The document also discusses routing micro-loops, which can occur briefly during convergence when different switches have inconsistent routing information. These are generally short-lived and acceptable in data center environments.
sections.eli5: When something breaks, the switches notice within seconds and find alternate routes. Because every switch talks to many others, one break does not isolate anyone.
